slides.title: Looks right, is wrong: money in a float
slides.tldr: A float cannot store most decimals exactly; tiny errors flip comparisons and lose cents until the books stop adding up. Never keep money in a float.

blocks.body: Press 0.1 + 0.2 on a pocket calculator and it shows 0.3. Your PHP code quietly keeps a slightly different number. Computers store decimals in **binary**, and 0.1 never ends in binary, just as 1 ÷ 3 never ends in decimal. So a `float` holds a very close number, not the exact one.

blocks.code:
$total = 0.10 + 0.20;           // 10 cents + 20 cents

var_dump($total == 0.30);       // bool(false)
echo $total;                    // 0.3 - looks fine
printf('%.20f', $total);        // 0.30000000000000004441

marks.tip: The sum is not equal to 0.30. A comparison like `if ($paid == $due)` can therefore make the wrong decision now and then.
This is the number actually stored. echo rounds it for display, which is why the error goes unnoticed.

blocks.code:
$total = 10 + 20;               // 10 cents + 20 cents, whole numbers

var_dump($total === 30);        // bool(true), every time

marks.tip: Whole numbers add exactly. Nothing is rounded, so nothing can disagree.

blocks.caption: How a tiny error grows into a real discrepancy

steps.title: 1. Add floats
steps.tip: In binary both 0.1 and 0.2 are approximations, so their sum is an approximation too.

steps.title: 2. Comparison breaks
steps.tip: Even the question "does the payment equal the amount due?" can get the wrong answer.

steps.title: 3. Cents go missing
steps.body: Small errors cut or flip whole cents
steps.tip: Ten 10-cent coins added one by one give 0.9999999999999999, not 1. And `(int)(0.57 * 100)` gives 56, not 57: a cent has vanished.

steps.title: 4. Books don't match
steps.body: At day end the bank and the ledger disagree
steps.tip: No exception, no log line, the totals just differ. This is the hardest kind of bug to track down.

blocks.body: Money is never a float. Never.

aside.title: Three days for a few cents
aside.body: An e-commerce company's end-of-day report came out $3.12 short of the bank's figure. It took three days to find the cause: one float multiplication in the sales tax calculation. There was no exception anywhere.

items.meaning: An approximate decimal number stored in binary; it cannot hold an exact money amount.

check.q: Printing 0.10 + 0.20 shows 0.3. Why can you still not trust it?
check.a: Printing rounds it for display. The stored value is 0.30000000000000004..., so `==` comparisons break and errors pile up over many transactions.

slides.title: Count the cents, and write the currency with it
slides.tldr: Store money as an integer in the smallest unit (the minor unit), and always keep the currency code next to the amount.

blocks.title: Counting at the cash counter
blocks.body: A cashier never counts "half a dollar"; they count 50 one-cent coins, a whole number. And the dollar drawer is separate from the euro drawer: put a note in the wrong one and the books go wrong. The **minor unit** is that smallest coin (cent), and the currency is the label on the drawer.

blocks.caption: The amount people see and the integer in the database

rows.tip: One cent is the minor unit of the US dollar. 1,250 dollars and 50 cents is 125050 cents.
The euro's minor unit is also the cent. 5 euros and 99 cents is 599 cents.
The yen has no fractional part, which is why assuming two decimal places for every currency is a mistake.
The Kuwaiti dinar has three decimal places. The ISO 4217 list tells you how many each currency has.

blocks.body: An amount is an integer minor unit plus a currency. The two are never separated.

aside.body: The float error and the question "which currency?" have one fix: keep an integer and a currency together in a single Money object.

items.meaning: The smallest unit of a currency: the cent for the dollar and the euro, the penny for the pound.
The international list of currencies (USD, EUR, JPY and so on), including how many decimal places each has.

items: Don't hardcode the number of decimal places; take the list from a library (for example `brick/money` or `moneyphp/money`).
A whole minor unit can't hold a price like 0.4 cents per API call. Keep a finer unit, such as millionths of a dollar, and round to cents once on the final bill.

check.q: You store both 500 yen and 500 dollars as `500` in the database. What gets lost?
check.a: The currency. A bare `500` doesn't say yen or dollars. And 500 dollars is really 50000 cents, so you also need to know the number of decimal places.

slides.title: The Money value object and Doctrine
slides.tldr: An immutable Money class holds an integer and a currency, checks the currency before adding, catches overflow, and maps to two Doctrine columns.

blocks.body: Bind the amount and currency together in a **value object**: it never changes after creation (`readonly`) and it refuses to do the wrong thing. Add USD to EUR and it throws an exception instead of quietly producing a wrong number.

marks.tip: `readonly` means the amount never changes once built. Adding returns a new Money.
When an int overflows, PHP silently turns it into a float. This one line catches that.
Matching the drawers: adding different currencies throws an exception instead of failing silently.
The column is BIGINT because a 32-bit INT stops at about 2.1 billion cents, which is only 21 million dollars. A busy wallet or company ledger can pass that.
Callers only ever see a Money; the two-column detail stays inside the entity.

items: In DBAL 4 a BIGINT column comes back as an `int`; older DBAL returns a string, so you need an `(int)` cast.
A `DECIMAL` column works too, but PHP hands it back as a string; an integer minor unit is simplest.

aside.body: Money is immutable: add and subtract return a new Money.

check.q: Money has `$amount` and `$currency` as public properties. Why is the class still safe?
check.a: The class is `readonly`, so nobody can change a value after it is built. And the add/subtract paths check the currency, so a wrong amount can never be created.

slides.title: Split money without losing a single cent
slides.tldr: Dividing money leaves a remainder; rounding every share the same way loses cents. Allocate instead, and put the remainder in someone's share.

blocks.body: Three friends are splitting a $100 restaurant bill. 100 ÷ 3 = 33.333..., so giving each 33.33 totals 99.99 and 1 cent belongs to nobody. Rounding share by share loses cents like this, or invents them: split six ways, rounding gives 1667 each, 10002 in all. The fix: first give everyone their floor share, then hand out the **remainder** one cent at a time.

blocks.code:
$share = (int) round(10000 / 3);          // 3333 cents
$parts = [$share, $share, $share];        // total 9999 - 1 cent vanished

marks.tip: We split $100 and got back $99.99. That missing cent is written down nowhere in the ledger.
intdiv cuts toward the lower number (the floor), so nobody gets too much. What was cut off is the remainder.
The remainder is always smaller than the number of ratios, so one cent each is enough to hand it all out.

blocks.caption: $100 (10000 cents) split three ways with allocate(1, 1, 1)

items.label: Friend 1
items.tip: The first friend got the 1 leftover cent. The rule for who gets it is fixed in advance.

items.label: Friend 3
items.tip: The floor share. The three shares add up to exactly 10000.

blocks.body: The parts always add up to the whole. The remainder has to land in someone's share.

items: When a percentage (fee, sales tax) produces a fraction, choose the rounding rule once (usually half-up) and keep it in one place.
Don't round step by step; do all the multiplying and dividing first, then round once at the end.
This `allocate` refuses negative amounts. To split a refund, allocate the positive amount and negate each share.
If an API sends amounts as a JSON number (12.5), JavaScript turns it into a float. Send an integer minor unit and a currency instead.

check.q: What does allocate return when $100 is split four ways in the ratio 1:1:1:1?
check.a: Each person gets $25 (2500 cents) with a remainder of 0. Split three ways, the 1 cent remainder goes to the first person: 3334, 3333, 3333.

slides.title: Just a balance column: "Where did my money go?"
slides.tldr: With only a balance number there is no history. When something is wrong, you can't tell who changed it, when, or why.

blocks.body: Rebecca calls support: "My wallet is $50 short. Who took it?" All the database holds is `balance = 1200`. Who lowered it, why, and when? None of that is written down. You can't even tell whether two concurrent requests overwrote each other. Forget getting the right figure; you can't find where the mistake happened.

blocks.file: What a CRUD app naturally writes
blocks.code:
UPDATE wallet
   SET balance = balance - 50
 WHERE id = 7;
-- The old amount? The reason? Who did it? All gone.

marks.tip: This line wipes the old number and writes the new one in its place. No history is left.

blocks.caption: A balance column alone vs a book of entries

columns.title: Balance column only
items: You can't tell who lowered it
After an error, you can't work out the right amount
You have nothing to show an auditor
columns.tip: Simple, but every change erases the information that came before it.

columns.title: A book of entries (ledger)
items: Every change has its own line
You can recompute the balance for any day
An auditor can check it line by line
columns.tip: Each transaction is a new line; the balance is the sum of those lines.

aside.title: Two bugs that canceled out
aside.body: In one app, a bug charged $20 too much and another charged $20 too little. Together they left the balance looking correct. With only a balance, nobody would ever have caught either one. Because entries existed, an auditor found both.
A balance is an answer, not history. Without history you can't check the answer.

check.q: After `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 50` runs, what information is lost?
check.a: The old amount, why it dropped, which transaction caused it and who did it. Only the new number remains, so nothing can be checked.

slides.title: Money moves from one account to another
slides.tldr: Every transaction has at least two entries: total debits always equal total credits; entries never change; the balance is computed from entries.

blocks.title: The bank passbook
blocks.body: Every line in a passbook is written in ink; nobody crosses one out and writes a new number. Each deposit or withdrawal also has a line on the other side, in someone else's book: money comes from somewhere and goes somewhere, and it never just evaporates. The current balance isn't written anywhere separately. It is whatever you get by adding up all the lines.

blocks.caption: Ryan sends Kevin $50 with a $1 fee (all amounts in dollars)

rows.tip: $51 leaves Ryan's wallet ($50 sent plus the $1 fee). A wallet is a liability for us, so a debit means the balance goes down.
$50 arrives in Kevin's wallet. The liability grows, so it is a credit.
$1 is added to our income book. Income also grows on the credit side.
If the two sides don't add up to the same number, the transaction is not accepted at all.

blocks.body: In every transaction, total debits = total credits. Entries are written, never edited or deleted.

items.meaning: One line on one side of an account: the account, debit or credit, and an amount.
The two sides of the book. On accounts like a wallet (our liability) or fee income, credit increases the balance and debit decreases it.
Not a separate number but one computed from the sum of the entries.

aside.body: Every amount has a source and a destination, so money that vanishes or appears from nowhere gets caught.

check.q: Ryan's wallet loses 51 and Kevin's gains 50. Where is the other 1 dollar, and why must it be written down?
check.a: In the fee income account, as a 1 credit. Without it, debits are 51 and credits 50, which is unbalanced, and nothing explains where the dollar went.

slides.title: Building the tables: account, transaction, entry
slides.tldr: Three tables: account, transaction, entry. CHECK, a currency foreign key and REVOKE block bad amounts, wrong-currency entries and edits; balance = SUM of entries.

blocks.body: Three tables are enough. An **account** is a page in the book, in one currency; a **transaction** is one event (one transfer), and an **entry** is each line of that event. The amount is always a positive integer; the `side` column says which direction. And the app's database user is never granted UPDATE or DELETE at all. The price: a mistake can only be fixed by a new reversing transaction, never by an edit.

marks.tip: `UNIQUE` means a transaction can be reversed at most once, which prevents a double reversal.
The amount is always above 0. The `side` decides whether the balance goes up or down, not a negative number.
The entry's currency must match its account's currency. An EUR entry on a USD wallet is rejected by the database itself.
The app's user can't change an entry, whether by mistake or through a bug. It's like a page written in ink.
Credit adds, debit subtracts. The sum is the balance, and no separate number is stored anywhere.

items: If you need the balance fast, keep a cached column, but treat it as a figure computed from entries, not the source of truth. If they disagree, the entries are right.
To enforce the "both sides are equal" rule in the database, use a `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` constraint trigger in PostgreSQL.

check.q: Why does ledger_entry have a `side` column instead of allowing a negative `amount_minor`?
check.a: To avoid mistakes about direction (such as a negative debit). The amount is always a positive integer, and the direction is written explicitly as D or C.

slides.title: The posting service: unbalanced means not written
slides.tldr: One service writes all entries in one transaction after checking debits = credits in each currency. A mistake is never deleted; you write a reversing transaction.

blocks.body: Every write goes through one door: `LedgerService::post()`. It first checks that the two sides add up in each currency, then writes the transaction and its entries in a single DB transaction. A wrong transaction can't be deleted or edited. Instead you write a **reversing entry**: a new transaction with every line on the opposite side.

marks.tip: Every currency must net to exactly zero on its own. 500 USD debited against 500 GBP credited leaves USD at +500 and GBP at -500, so it is refused. See the next slide.
The transaction and all its entries go in together. If it fails halfway, nothing is written and no half transaction is left behind.
For a reversal, the original transaction's id goes here; the UNIQUE constraint prevents reversing it twice.

blocks.file: Reversing: an opposite entry, not a delete

marks.tip: `reversed()` turns each line's debit into a credit and its credit into a debit. The amounts stay the same.
The link to the original transaction is recorded, so an auditor can see the two as a pair.

blocks.caption: Effect on Ryan's wallet, Kevin's wallet and fee income (in dollars)

rows.tip: The original transaction, which was a mistake. It stays in the book forever.
Every line is the opposite. #1 is not deleted; its effect is canceled out.
After both transactions everyone's balance is as before, and history still shows both lines.

items: Never run UPDATE or DELETE on a wrong entry. Nobody will ever know what really happened.
After a reversal, write the corrected transaction separately; reversing and correcting are two steps, not one.

check.q: What is the benefit of writing an opposite entry instead of deleting a wrong transaction?
check.a: History stays intact: both the original mistake and its reversal are visible. An auditor can see what happened, when, and how it was corrected.

slides.title: Debits equal credits in every currency
slides.tldr: Adding amounts without looking at the currency lets a 500 USD debit and a 500 GBP credit pass as balanced. Each currency must balance alone; a conversion goes through FX accounts.

blocks.body: A transfer is posted as 500 USD debited from Ryan and 500 GBP credited to Kevin. A check that only adds the plain numbers sees 50000 = 50000 and accepts it. But 500 GBP is about 625 USD at 1.25 dollars to the pound, so the bank just handed over 125 dollars for nothing. You can't add a dollar bill to a pound note and call it a total.

marks.tip: Two different currencies. With a total that ignores the currency, this is accepted and money appears from nowhere.

blocks.caption: The right way: Ryan pays 625 USD, Kevin receives 500 GBP (1 GBP = 1.25 USD)

rows.tip: Ryan's dollars leave his wallet.
The bank's own dollar account takes the dollars in. Now the USD side has both a debit and a credit.
The bank's own pound account gives the pounds out.
Kevin's wallet receives the pounds.
The USD entries balance on their own.
The GBP entries balance on their own. Both currencies pass the check.

blocks.body: Debits equal credits in every currency, not in total.

items: The price: you need an FX clearing account per currency, and the rate used must be stored with the transaction (for example in the memo), or nobody can audit the conversion later.
The database backs this up: an entry's currency must equal its account's currency, so a GBP entry can never land on a USD wallet.

check.q: Why is a USD 500 debit with a GBP 500 credit refused, and how do you post a real conversion?
check.a: USD nets to +500 and GBP to -500, so neither balances. Post four entries through FX clearing accounts, so each currency has its own debit and credit that match.

slides.title: The gateway says 1000, my books say 997
slides.tldr: Your own ledger and the outside statement are two separate truths. If nobody compares them, missing or extra transactions hide for months.

blocks.body: At month end the gateway's statement shows 1000 successful payments, but our ledger has 997. There's no error log and no customer complaint. Three people were charged, yet their orders are still "pending". The reason: the gateway took the money and sent its reply, but our server timed out at that exact moment.

blocks.caption: The money was taken, but we never found out

actors.label: Our app
actors.tip: Calls the gateway for the customer's payment. Records "pending" in its own ledger.

actors.label: Gateway
actors.tip: Takes the money from the bank. Records the transaction as "paid" in its own statement.

messages.label: Success (but lost on the way)
messages.tip: Our app timed out and never received the reply.
The outside truth and our truth are now different.

blocks.body: Your books and the outside books are two separate truths. Without regular matching, errors quietly pile up.

aside.title: A surprise six months later
aside.body: A company learned in its annual audit, six months on, that the gateway showed $12,000 more than its own records. A retry bug had meant some payments were never written to the ledger. Daily matching would have caught it on day one.
Outside systems (banks, gateways) keep their own version of the truth. Unless you regularly check that your books agree with theirs, you won't know.

check.q: There is no error log and nobody complained. How can 3 payments still be out of step?
check.a: The gateway took the money, but we never got the reply, so our ledger stayed "pending". No exception was raised in the code; the two books simply differ.

slides.title: The matching key and six kinds of break
slides.tldr: Join every line in the two books with an immutable reference. Anything that doesn't join, or doesn't agree on amount, is a break.

blocks.title: A shop owner's closing time
blocks.body: At night, a shop owner checks every line of their own sales notebook against the card processor's daily statement. The key they match on is the transaction ID, not the time or the amount, because many transactions share the same amount. Whatever doesn't match gets circled in red ink. That red circle is a **break**.

blocks.caption: Types of break and their likely causes

rows.tip: The money was taken and we don't know it. The most dangerous type.
We assumed the payment went through; the gateway knows nothing about it. Releasing the goods is a loss.
The reference matched but the amount didn't. Often down to a fee or a currency difference.
The same transaction was counted twice, usually when idempotency isn't right.

cells: A refund or chargeback we never saw
rows.tip: The amount agrees but the status doesn't, for example refunded at the gateway but paid in our books.
Not a real error, just a difference in which day it falls on. It matches in the next day's statement.

items.meaning: A line that doesn't match between the two books. One break means one investigation to do.
An immutable reference that identifies the same transaction on both sides, such as the gateway's payment id.

items: Save the gateway reference in your own table at the moment you create the payment. It is hard to find later.
Flag timing breaks separately, so they don't raise false alarms every day.

check.q: Why match on a reference id rather than "compare the amount and the time"?
check.a: Many transactions can share an amount and a time, so matching on those pairs up the wrong ones. A reference id is unique per transaction.

slides.title: The daily job: fetch the statement, match, write breaks
slides.tldr: Load the statement into a table, find all six break types with one FULL OUTER JOIN, and run a console command every morning with the Symfony Scheduler.

blocks.body: The method has three steps. First, load the provider's statement (file or API) into a `statement_line` table. Second, run one `FULL OUTER JOIN` against `ledger_payment`, with each ref counted per side and compared on amount, status and day. Anything missing on a side, counted twice, or different is a break, and the `CASE` names which of the six it is. A line whose reference matches but lands on a different day is a `timing` break. To tell that from a truly missing line, the query looks one day either side, so the job runs for two days ago, when the neighboring day's statement has arrived. Third, write the results to `recon_break` with a UNIQUE on `(day, provider, ref)`, so that running the job twice never inserts the same break twice.

blocks.code:
-- :from = :day - 1, :to = :day + 1 (one day either side, to spot timing)
WITH l AS (SELECT ref, MIN(day) day, COUNT(*) n, MAX(amount_minor) amt, MAX(status) st
             FROM ledger_payment  WHERE day BETWEEN :from AND :to GROUP BY ref),
     s AS (SELECT ref, MIN(day) day, COUNT(*) n, MAX(amount_minor) amt, MAX(status) st
             FROM statement_line WHERE day BETWEEN :from AND :to GROUP BY ref)
INSERT INTO recon_break (day, provider, ref, category, our_minor, their_minor)
SELECT :day, 'gw', COALESCE(l.ref, s.ref),
       CASE WHEN l.n > 1 OR s.n > 1 THEN 'duplicate'
            WHEN s.ref IS NULL      THEN 'missing_at_provider'
            WHEN l.ref IS NULL      THEN 'missing_in_ledger'
            WHEN l.amt <> s.amt     THEN 'amount_mismatch'
            WHEN l.st  <> s.st      THEN 'status_mismatch'
            ELSE 'timing' END,
       l.amt, s.amt
  FROM l FULL OUTER JOIN s ON s.ref = l.ref
 WHERE COALESCE(l.day, s.day) = :day
   AND (l.n > 1 OR s.n > 1 OR l.ref IS NULL OR s.ref IS NULL
        OR l.amt <> s.amt OR l.st <> s.st OR l.day <> s.day)
ON CONFLICT (day, provider, ref) DO NOTHING;

marks.tip: Per side: how many lines carry this ref (`n`), plus its amount, status and day. `n` above 1 is a duplicate.
The CASE runs top to bottom. The first test that is true names the break. Whatever survives all five is the same ref on a different day: timing.
Keep only breaks that belong to this day (the ledger side's day wins), so the next day's run does not report the same line again.
On a second run the same break is not inserted again, so the job is safe to re-run.
The Symfony Scheduler runs this command every day at 3 a.m. To keep it running you need `messenger:consume scheduler_default`.
Without an argument it means "2 days ago", when the neighboring day's statement has arrived. You can also re-run any earlier day by hand.

items: Send an alert when the break count is above 0. If it stays silent, nobody will look.
Index `(day, ref)` on both tables or the join scans everything. A few million lines a day is fine; far beyond that, partition by day.
For how the statement file gets fetched, see [[ledgers/batch-files/half-loaded-file|Batch file integration]].

check.q: Why is `recon_break` UNIQUE on `(day, provider, ref)`, and why `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`?
check.a: If the job runs twice (a retry, or by hand), the same break would be inserted twice. UNIQUE plus DO NOTHING makes the job safe to run again and again.

slides.title: Don't edit your books to hide a gap
slides.tldr: Updating the ledger to close a break is wrong. Open the break, find the cause, then close it with a correcting entry.

blocks.body: The easy temptation when you see a gap: "The bank's figure must be right, so I'll just put it in the ledger." The numbers now match, but the reason for the mistake is buried for good. The right way: keep the break open, find the cause, then write a new correcting entry and close the break.

marks.tip: The old amount is gone. Why it was wrong and who changed it can never be known.
Who, when and why are recorded on the break itself. That is the evidence of the investigation.
The mistake is fixed in a new transaction; no earlier entry changes. The two sides add up, as always.
The break is linked to the transaction that closed it, so an auditor can go straight there later.

blocks.caption: The life of a break

steps.title: 1. Open
steps.body: The nightly job writes the break; nobody has looked yet
steps.tip: In this state the break counts as outstanding; old open breaks are the real risk.

steps.title: 2. Investigating
steps.body: An owner finds the cause and writes it down
steps.tip: A break with no owner gets no attention, so naming one is mandatory.

steps.title: 3. Resolved
steps.body: A new entry is written and linked to the break
steps.tip: The ledger changes only by adding a new entry.

steps.title: 4. Written off
steps.body: A small amount, closed with a second person's approval
steps.tip: You can't chase a tiny amount forever. It is posted to a write-off account as a normal entry, and the decision is written down and approved.

items: If open breaks pile up, eventually nobody looks at them. Alert on age (for example, older than 3 days).

check.q: If you run an UPDATE to make the ledger match the statement, what exactly is lost?
check.a: The cause of the gap and its history. The numbers match, but if the same bug happens again there is no way to catch it.

slides.title: An outside service slowed down, and our site stopped
slides.tldr: Without a timeout, every worker gets stuck on the outside call. Once a vendor slows down, your whole site is dead within seconds.

blocks.body: The night before a Black Friday sale, the payment gateway suddenly slows to 30 seconds per call. We have 50 PHP workers and 10 checkout requests per second. Within 5 seconds, every worker is stuck waiting on the gateway. Pages that have nothing to do with the gateway, like the home page and user profiles, stop responding too.

blocks.caption: One slow vendor, and every worker on the site is stuck

nodes.label: Users
nodes.tip: The night before the Black Friday sale, lots of users hit checkout at the same moment.

nodes.label: 50 PHP workers
nodes.tip: Each worker holds one request at a time. While it is stuck, it can't take anyone new.

nodes.label: Gateway
nodes.tip: A system outside our control. When it is slow, we can't fix it.

edges.label: Each worker calls the gateway and sits waiting for the reply
The reply comes after 30 seconds, by which time 10 × 30 requests have piled up
All 50 workers are used up within 5 seconds; every page on the site returns errors

marks.tip: By default it waits up to about 60 seconds (`default_socket_timeout`). With a slow vendor, that is far too long.
Until the reply arrives, the worker can't do anything else. When all workers are stuck here, the site is dead.

blocks.body: An outside service will be slow one day. Never make an outside call without a timeout.

aside.body: We can't make the vendor faster. What we can do is make sure its slowness doesn't trap our workers.

items.meaning: The longest we are willing to wait. When it passes, the call is canceled, we catch the error and move on.

check.q: When the gateway is slow, why does the home page die as well as checkout?
check.a: The slow calls hold every worker. There is no free worker left to take the home page request.

slides.title: Symfony HttpClient: timeouts and retries done right
slides.tldr: Web requests get a short timeout and no retries; queue workers get retries with backoff. Tell transport errors apart from 4xx; retry a POST only with an idempotency key.

blocks.body: Build **scoped clients** for the vendor, with the base URL, key, timeout and retry settings in one place. **timeout** is the longest the server may stay silent, while **max_duration** caps the whole request. Retries need care. With `max_duration: 3` and 10 checkouts a second, a web request holds at most 10 × 3 = 30 of your 50 workers. Add 3 retries and one request can hold a worker for over 15 seconds, and the site is dead again. So the web client never retries; the queue-worker client does, with a growing wait (**exponential backoff**) and a little randomness (**jitter**), or everyone hits the vendor at the same moment.

blocks.code:
framework:
  http_client:
    scoped_clients:
      gateway.client:               # web requests: fail fast, never retry
        base_uri: '%env(GATEWAY_URL)%'
        auth_bearer: '%env(GATEWAY_KEY)%'
        timeout: 2          # longest silence allowed (seconds)
        max_duration: 3     # cap for the whole request
      gateway.worker_client:        # queue workers: patient, with retries
        base_uri: '%env(GATEWAY_URL)%'
        auth_bearer: '%env(GATEWAY_KEY)%'
        timeout: 3
        max_duration: 10
        retry_failing:
          max_retries: 3
          delay: 500        # first wait (ms)
          multiplier: 2     # 500, 1000, 2000
          jitter: 0.3       # random +/-30%
          http_codes: [429, 502, 503, 504]

marks.tip: If the server sends nothing for 2 seconds, a TransportException is thrown. The worker is no longer stuck.
Even if the server trickles out its reply, we never wait longer than 3 seconds. 10 requests a second hold at most 30 workers, so 20 stay free.
Without random gaps, thousands of clients retry at the same instant and knock the vendor down again.
The `gateway.client` scoped client is injected automatically into the argument named `$gatewayClient`. The worker one would be `$gatewayWorkerClient`.
If a POST is ever retried (by the worker client, or by us later), the money could be taken twice. So the same Idempotency-Key goes out every time.
A timeout or a 5xx doesn't mean "failed", it means "we don't know". That state needs its own handling.
A 4xx means our request itself was wrong or rejected. Retrying won't help.

items: Don't retry every error. Retrying a 4xx (a bad request) just repeats the same mistake.
Never retry inside a web request: 4 attempts of 3 seconds hold a worker for 15 seconds or more. Retry from a queue worker.

items.label: The "we don't know" state after a timeout

check.q: What goes wrong if you leave out `jitter` on retries, and which header matters when retrying a POST?
check.a: Thousands of clients retry at the same instant and knock the vendor down again. On a POST, send the same Idempotency-Key so the money isn't taken twice.

slides.title: Rate limits: the delivery office's busy phone line
slides.tldr: A vendor accepts a limited number of calls per second. Stop on a 429, and also pace your own calls with the Symfony RateLimiter.

blocks.title: The delivery office phone line
blocks.body: A delivery company's dispatch office can only answer so many calls at once. Phone them 100 times in a minute and they'll block your number. A smart customer sets their own pace: at most 20 calls a minute, and a short wait when they hear "busy". That self-imposed pace is a client-side rate limiter.

blocks.caption: Our own limiter stops us first; if a 429 still comes, we wait

nodes.label: Our app
nodes.tip: Before calling the vendor, it asks the limiter, "May I send now?"

nodes.label: RateLimiter
nodes.tip: A token bucket: 50 tokens are added every second. With no token, you wait.

nodes.label: Gateway
nodes.tip: The vendor's own limit. We want to stay below it.

edges.label: Asks for a token before the call
With a token, the call goes through
If a 429 still comes back, the app waits before retrying

blocks.code:
framework:
  rate_limiter:
    gateway_outgoing:
      policy: 'token_bucket'
      limit: 50
      rate: { interval: '1 second', amount: 50 }

marks.tip: The bucket holds at most 50 tokens. In a sudden rush that many calls can go out at once.
50 tokens are added back every second. This is the long-run pace.
The config name `gateway_outgoing` is injected automatically as `$gatewayOutgoingLimiter`.
If it would need to wait over 2 seconds, an exception is thrown. The worker never sleeps indefinitely.

items: In a web request, reply with a 503 straight away instead of calling `wait()`; long waits belong in a queue worker.
The limiter's state lives in the cache, so several servers together respect the same limit.

check.q: The vendor's limit is 60/second. Why set our own limiter to 50?
check.a: Staying below the limit means you almost never see a 429. Run right at the limit and the vendor blocks you at the slightest rush.

slides.title: Keep the vendor behind your own interface
slides.tldr: The domain only knows its own `PaymentGateway` interface; the vendor's language lives in a single adapter, so changing vendor leaves the rest of the code alone.

blocks.body: Without a wall around it, Acme's `state` field and its error codes spread through checkout, refunds and reports. The day Acme doubles its fee, every one of those places has to be found and rewritten. That is **vendor lock-in**.

blocks.title: The wall socket and the adapter
blocks.body: Every appliance in your house plugs into the same standard socket. If you travel with a foreign plug, you put an adapter in between and the appliance itself doesn't change. In code, the **interface** is the socket and the **adapter** is that travel adapter. When the vendor changes, only the adapter changes.

blocks.caption: The domain knows only the interface, nothing about the vendor

nodes.label: Checkout
nodes.tip: The business rules live here. No vendor name, field or error code gets in.

nodes.label: PaymentGateway
nodes.tip: Our own socket: charge(ChargeRequest): ChargeResult. The shape is the same whichever vendor sits behind it.

nodes.label: AcmePayGateway
nodes.tip: Translates Acme's JSON, fields and error codes into our language.

nodes.label: OtherPayGateway
nodes.tip: When the vendor changes, only this new adapter has to be written.

edges.label: Today, Acme's adapter sits behind the interface
Tomorrow, another vendor can be plugged in here

marks.tip: The interface contains only our own types: ChargeRequest and ChargeResult. Nothing from Acme.
Acme's "state" field and its "paid" value are translated into our enum in this one place only.

blocks.title: A plan for leaving the vendor (exit plan)
items: Store the vendor's name and the vendor reference for every transaction in your own table.
Get the right to export the vendor's data (customers, tokens, history) written into the contract.
Write the new vendor's adapter and run it side by side with the old one for a while.

use: A vendor that is costly or risky to change (payments, SMS, email)
avoid: A small one-off tool, where a whole adapter layer is needless extra work

check.q: When the vendor changes, why does only one class change?
check.a: The vendor's fields, errors and vocabulary exist only in the adapter. The rest of the code knows our own interface and types, so it never has to be touched.

slides.title: The fee rise: what the adapter buys and what it costs
slides.tldr: With an adapter, a vendor swap is one new class and one changed alias. The price is extra code and an interface limited to what every vendor offers. Use it where leaving would hurt.

blocks.body: Acme emails: its fee rises from 1.5% to 2.5% next month. You send about $2,000,000 a month through it, so that is $20,000 more every month. A rival offers 1.2%, which would save $26,000 a month against the new price. Without an adapter, `$raw['state']` and Acme's error codes sit in some 40 files, and switching is a months-long refactor, so you pay the rise. With the adapter, you write `OtherPayGateway`, run it beside the old one, and flip one line.

blocks.code:
services:
    App\Payment\PaymentGateway:
        alias: App\Payment\OtherPayGateway   # was AcmePayGateway

marks.tip: The only line that changes. Every class that asks for `PaymentGateway` now gets the new adapter.

blocks.caption: The adapter: what you gain and what you pay

columns.title: What it buys
items: A vendor change touches one class, not 40 files
A real alternative when negotiating the fee
Tests use a fake gateway, with no network
columns.tip: The gain shows up on the day you have to leave a vendor.

columns.title: What it costs
items: An interface, an adapter and tests to write and keep up to date
Only features every vendor has fit the interface
Guess the interface from one vendor and it copies that vendor, fitting no other
columns.tip: Paid every day, whether or not you ever switch.

blocks.body: Wrap the vendors that would hurt to leave. Call the rest directly.

use: Money, SMS, email or identity checks: costly to leave, with real rivals
avoid: A one-off tool, or a vendor with no alternative: the adapter is code you never use

items: Shape the interface around what your domain needs (charge, refund, status), not around Acme's API.
Write one contract test that every adapter must pass. That is how you know the new vendor really behaves the same.

check.q: Name one thing the adapter buys you and one thing it costs.
check.a: Buys: a vendor change touches one class. Costs: extra code and tests, and only the features every vendor shares fit the interface.

slides.title: Fine in the sandbox, broken in production
slides.tldr: The sandbox is fast, always succeeds and has no crowd; production is slow, failing and limited. Code tested only in the sandbox gets a surprise in production.

blocks.body: The sandbox is the vendor's playground: fake data, fake money, never a crowd. Code that passes tests there takes its first real hit from real customers. If you know the likely differences up front, launch day holds fewer surprises.

blocks.caption: Typical differences between sandbox and production

rows.tip: A timeout never happens in the sandbox, so your timeout code never gets tested.
Real cards and banks reject payments for many reasons. The failure paths are most of production's work.
Limits can differ in production; check the contract or the dashboard.

cells: Late, twice, or out of order
rows.tip: Real webhooks come with retries, duplicates and delays.
The keys differ, so there is a risk of putting the wrong key in the wrong env.

blocks.code:
# .env holds only the sandbox default (committed)
GATEWAY_URL=https://sandbox.acmepay.example/v2

# production keys never go in a file, only in the secrets vault
php bin/console secrets:set GATEWAY_KEY --env=prod
php bin/console secrets:set GATEWAY_URL --env=prod

marks.tip: With the sandbox as the default, nobody can move real money by accident from a local machine.
The real key lives in the vault and never reaches git.

blocks.body: The sandbox only tests that the pieces connect. Simulate timeouts, failures and duplicates yourself.

items: In tests, build the slow or failing vendor yourself: Symfony's `MockHttpClient` can fake timeouts, 429s and 503s.
On launch day, watch the first few real transactions yourself, and keep the [[ledgers/reconciliation/three-missing-payments|reconciliation]] job running.

check.q: Why does timeout code never get tested in the sandbox, and how will you test it?
check.a: The sandbox always answers quickly, so a timeout never happens. Test it by faking slow or failing responses with `MockHttpClient`.

slides.title: Half the file loaded, then a crash
slides.tldr: Read a file without checking it arrived whole, or stop at one bad row, and you get a half load, and a double load when you run it again.

blocks.body: Every night the bank drops a salary CSV on SFTP, and our cron job reads it and credits the wallets. One night the file was still uploading and the cron read half of it. Another night, row 4000 had a strange character in a name and the loop crashed right there: 3999 people got paid and the rest didn't. In the morning someone ran it again, and the first 3999 people were paid a second time.

blocks.caption: Three mistakes with the nightly file, and nobody noticed

actors.label: Bank (SFTP)
actors.tip: Uploads the file. The upload takes time, and the file is visible while it is half done.

actors.label: Our cron
actors.tip: Looks for the file at 2 a.m. on its own schedule. Never checks whether the file is complete.

actors.label: Wallet
actors.tip: Credits whatever it is given; if it gets a double, it pays double.

messages.label: Reads half the file and credits it

messages.note: The other half of the users got no money

messages.label: Next night: crash at row 4000
messages.tip: One bad row stopped the whole loop.

messages.label: Re-run in the morning, from the start

messages.note: The first 3999 people were paid twice
messages.tip: Re-running wasn't safe, because nothing recorded which rows had already been loaded.

blocks.body: Not one row gets loaded until the file is proven complete and intact.

aside.body: With file-based integrations you must settle three questions in advance: "Did it arrive whole?", "Did this same file come before?" and "What do we do with a bad row?"

items.meaning: A large file that arrives once or a few times a day, holding thousands of transactions at once.

check.q: Why did the first 3999 people get paid twice in the second incident?
check.a: After the crash there was no record of which rows had already been loaded. So when it ran again, the file was read from the start.

slides.title: The packing slip: checksum and control total
slides.tldr: Four gates before you read a file: did it arrive whole, does the checksum match, does the control total match, has it come before.

blocks.title: A package's packing slip
blocks.body: A delivery box has a packing slip on it: "3 items, total value $175.00, seal number 457". You open the box, count and add up, and compare; if it doesn't match, the box goes back. The **trailer** line at the end of a file is that slip: the **control total** (the number of rows and the total amount), while the **checksum** is the seal, which tells you whether the file changed on the way.

marks.tip: The header: who sent it, which date, which version of the format.
The trailer: 2 rows, 175050 cents in total. We count and add these two numbers ourselves to compare.

blocks.caption: Four gates before loading a file

steps.title: 1. Fully arrived?
steps.body: Is there an end-of-upload marker (rename or .done)?
steps.tip: The sender uploads the file as .tmp and renames it at the end. We pick up only files with the final name.

steps.title: 2. Checksum matches?
steps.body: Is our own SHA-256 the same as the one sent?
steps.tip: If even one bit changed on the way, the hash differs, so a damaged file is caught.

steps.title: 3. Control total matches?
steps.body: Our own row count and sum = the trailer's numbers
steps.tip: This tells you whether the file was cut short or rows went missing.

steps.title: 4. Seen before?
steps.body: Has this hash already been fully loaded?
steps.tip: A file marked loaded is quietly skipped. One stuck half-way is resumed, not skipped.

blocks.body: If the file's own count and sum don't match the trailer, the whole file goes back.

items.meaning: A short fingerprint (hash) made from the file's contents; change one character and the fingerprint changes.
The row count and sum written in the file itself, which we count separately and compare.

items: On SFTP, ask the sender to upload as `.tmp` and rename at the end. Otherwise you risk grabbing a half-uploaded file.

check.q: The control total doesn't match, but 95% of the rows are fine. Can you load part of it?
check.a: No. A mismatch means the file may be truncated, altered or missing rows. We don't know which, so we send the whole file back and ask the sender for a new one.

slides.title: Past the gates, row by row: Symfony code
slides.tldr: Verify the hash and control total, claim the file, then load row by row. Bad rows go to quarantine; parse CSV and fixed-width into integer minor units.

blocks.body: The importer doesn't pull the whole file into memory at once; it reads one row at a time (a generator or `SplFileObject`). Each row is loaded in its own small transaction, and a bad row throws `InvalidRow` and goes to quarantine while the rest carry on. Any other crash stops the run, but the file stays marked `loading`, so the next run picks it up (next slide).

marks.tip: Does the SHA-256 we calculated match the one the sender gave? `hash_equals` is a timing-safe comparison.
`claim()` returns the file id for a new file, or for one still `loading` after a crash. For a `loaded` or `rejected` file it returns null.
`$file->count` and `totalMinor` are the numbers written in the trailer. If they differ from our own count, nothing is loaded.
A bad row doesn't stop the run; it goes elsewhere with its reason, and the rest of the file carries on.
In fixed-width, each field's start and length are written in the sender's spec. Cut by the spec, never by guesswork.
A regex checks the pattern; if it fails, this row goes to quarantine.
Only integer multiplication and addition; there is no float anywhere.

items: Convert a fixed-width file to UTF-8 before reading it (`mb_convert_encoding`); otherwise the character positions get thrown off.
To fetch files over SFTP, Flysystem's SFTP adapter works well; copy the file into your own directory first, and read it only from there.

items.label: Writes that are safe to do twice

check.q: What is the risk if the importer reads the whole file at once with `file()`, and what should you do?
check.a: It can run out of memory. Read one row at a time (a generator or `SplFileObject`) and load each row in its own small transaction.

slides.title: Crash at row 4000? The re-run finishes the file
slides.tldr: Give the file a status (`loading` until done) and give every row a tick written with its credit. A re-run skips loaded files, resumes half-loaded ones and skips ticked rows.

blocks.body: Back to the crash at row 4000. A re-run that skips every file it has seen would leave the file half loaded forever. So the file carries a status: `loading` until its last row is done, then `loaded`. A re-run skips only `loaded` files. And each row gets a tick in `batch_row`, written in the same transaction as its credit, like a payroll clerk ticking each name on the payout list: after a power outage she never pays a ticked name twice.

marks.tip: The tick table. Its primary key makes a second tick for the same row impossible.
Only `loading` files come back. `loaded` and `rejected` files return nothing, so they are skipped.
The tick was already there, so this row was credited in the earlier run. Do nothing.
The tick and the credit commit together or not at all. A crash can never leave one without the other.

blocks.caption: The morning re-run, same file, same crash point

actors.label: Our cron
actors.tip: Runs the importer again on the same file.

actors.label: batch_file
actors.tip: Remembers each file's status: loading, loaded or rejected.

actors.label: Wallet
actors.tip: Credits money. Now guarded by the per-row tick.

messages.label: Status is loading: carry on
messages.tip: The old code would have returned here and left the file half loaded.

items: Price: one extra INSERT per row, and `batch_row` grows with every file. Delete the ticks of files loaded months ago.
If two cron runs can overlap, take a Symfony Lock on the file hash first; otherwise both run and the second just waits on the first's ticks.
Skip the ticks when the credit is already idempotent on its own, for example an UPSERT keyed by `(file_id, line_no)`.

check.q: The importer crashed at row 4000 of 10,000. What does the next run do with rows 1-3999 and with row 4000?
check.a: It claims the file because its status is still `loading`. Rows 1-3999 find their tick and are skipped; row 4000 onwards are credited and ticked.

slides.title: Bad rows: not silently dropped, but set aside
slides.tldr: Catching and calling `continue` makes bad rows vanish. Keep them in a quarantine table with the reason, fix them, then re-run only those rows.

blocks.body: If one apple in a basket is rotten, you don't throw away the whole basket. But if you quietly toss the rotten one, nobody knows how many went. The right way: put the rotten one in a separate basket with a note on it saying why. Later, fix it and put it back with the good ones.

marks.tip: How many rows, which ones and why they were dropped: none of it is recorded. If somebody's money goes missing, there is no way to investigate.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE batch_file (
  id       bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  provider text     NOT NULL,
  name     text     NOT NULL,
  sha256   char(64) NOT NULL,
  status   text     NOT NULL DEFAULT 'received',
  UNIQUE (provider, sha256)
);
CREATE TABLE batch_row_error (
  file_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES batch_file (id),
  line_no int    NOT NULL,
  raw     text   NOT NULL,
  reason  text   NOT NULL,
  status  text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  PRIMARY KEY (file_id, line_no)
);

-- after fixing, just the open rows again
SELECT line_no, raw FROM batch_row_error
 WHERE file_id = :id AND status = 'open';

marks.tip: Stops the same file being taken twice. This one constraint is idempotency at the file level.
(file, row number) is unique. Re-running the same row doesn't create a second error row.

blocks.caption: Two ways to handle a bad row

columns.title: Silently dropped
items: You don't know how many rows were dropped
The reason is written nowhere
No way to fix them and run again
columns.tip: Quick to write, but it keeps no track of money that went missing.

columns.title: Quarantine
items: Which row, why, all recorded
The rest of the file isn't held up
Once fixed, only that row runs again
columns.tip: Every bad row has an address, a reason and a status.

items: Count what percentage of rows went to quarantine and alert on it. If it suddenly hits 20%, the problem isn't the file, it's our parser.
If the rows depend on each other (for example, parts of one calculation), use all-or-nothing instead.

check.q: Why does it matter that quarantine has `(file_id, line_no)` as its PRIMARY KEY?
check.a: If the file is run again, the same row doesn't get a second error row. Re-running stays safe.

slides.title: One book in everyone's hands: the shared database
slides.tldr: When several apps write straight into the same database tables, every column becomes a secret API. One person renames a column and the others break.

blocks.body: A hardware store has a single ledger, and the owner, her son and the accountant all write in it. One day the son renames the "Price" column to "Price (in cents)". The accountant's addition formula breaks, and nobody warned him. The same thing happens with apps when two of them reach straight into the same `orders` table.

blocks.caption: Three apps share one table: one changes it and the others break

nodes.label: Checkout
nodes.tip: The real owner of the orders table. Wants to move the money column from float to an integer in cents.

nodes.label: Reporting
nodes.tip: Reads from orders with its own SQL. The owner has no idea which columns it uses.

nodes.label: orders table
nodes.tip: Any app reads or writes here. No middleman, no contract.

nodes.label: Warehouse
nodes.tip: Runs UPDATE on orders.status directly, ignoring any of Checkout's rules.

edges.label: The nightly report's SQL can't find `total` and breaks
Warehouse sets `status = shipped`, even though the order is unpaid
edges.tip: Checkout's rule ("never shipped before payment") is something the warehouse knows nothing about.

blocks.body: Every column in a shared table is a secret API whose contract nobody knows.

aside.body: The apps have to talk to each other somehow. The question is how, and how tightly that ties us together.

items.meaning: A measure of how much breaks in one part when another part changes.

check.q: When two apps write to the same table, why does Checkout's "never shipped before payment" rule break?
check.a: The rule lives in Checkout's code, not in the table. Warehouse writes straight to the table and walks around that code.

slides.title: Four ways to communicate, and what they cost
slides.tldr: Four ways for apps to talk: shared DB, RPC, messaging, files. The more direct the link, the tighter the coupling.

blocks.title: Four kinds of contact at a hardware store
blocks.body: One ledger in everyone's hands is the closest and riskiest (shared DB). A direct phone call gets you an answer right away, but the other end must pick up (RPC). A letter in the mailbox is read later, so nobody is left waiting (messaging). A big box from the daily delivery truck carries a lot at once, but arrives late (file transfer).

blocks.caption: Four styles, five yardsticks

rows.tip: These are the "contract". Whatever is shared is hard to change.
The faster you need the answer, the more both sides must be running at once.

cells: If the other side is down
If the DB is held, both are down
rows.tip: With RPC, their problem becomes mine; with messaging and files, it doesn't.
How much I break when the other side changes.
Each style has a hidden price. Know it before you choose.

blocks.body: The less each side has to know, the looser the tie. Knowing another app's tables is the tightest tie of all.

items.meaning: Calling another app's function directly (usually over HTTP) and waiting for the reply.
Leaving a message on a queue; the other side picks it up and works on it in its own time.

aside.body: What you share is your contract; the smaller the contract, the looser the tie.

check.q: If the other app is down, why do RPC and messaging end up differently?
check.a: With RPC, my call fails at once because I need the reply. With messaging, the message waits in the queue and gets read when the other side is back up.

slides.title: One job, two ways: RPC and messaging
slides.tldr: With RPC you get an answer now but the other side must be up. With Messenger you leave a message and move on, and the other service handles it in its own time.

blocks.body: When an order is placed, the warehouse has to set the goods aside. With **RPC**, we call the warehouse directly and stop to wait for its answer. With **messaging**, we just leave the news "an order was placed" and the warehouse picks it up later. In the second way, even if the warehouse is down, our order isn't held up.

marks.tip: On this line the warehouse must be up. If it is down or slow, our order gets stuck too.
The message goes on the queue and the call returns straight away. Even with the warehouse down, the order succeeds.
The handler can run in a separate process or service. The same message can occasionally arrive twice, so keep this idempotent as well.

items.meaning: Safe to run twice: the second run changes nothing, like pressing an elevator button again.
How long we wait for a reply before giving up.

items: In messaging, a message can arrive "twice". If the handler isn't idempotent, the work is done twice.
Nesting RPC inside RPC (A→B→C) means one delay holds up the whole chain.

items.label: How many times a message arrives

check.q: The warehouse service is down for 10 minutes. What happens to new orders under RPC and under messaging?
check.a: Under RPC, orders hang or fail. Under messaging, the order succeeds, the message waits, and the warehouse catches up when it is back.

slides.title: Making "leave it and move on" real: routing
slides.tldr: With no routing line, Messenger runs the handler on the spot, so a dead warehouse still fails the order. One line of config sends the message to a queue instead.

blocks.body: Calling `dispatch()` doesn't make anything asynchronous by itself. With no routing rule, Messenger runs the handler right there in the same request, so a warehouse that is down still fails our order, exactly like RPC. A routing rule says "this message goes on the `async` queue", and a separate worker process picks it up. Retries and a failure transport (a shelf for messages that keep failing) live in the same file.

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        transports:
            async:
                dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
                retry_strategy:
                    max_retries: 3
                    delay: 1000        # 1s, then 2s, then 4s
                    multiplier: 2
            failed: 'doctrine://default?queue_name=failed'
        failure_transport: failed
        routing:
            App\Message\OrderPlaced: async

marks.tip: If the warehouse is down, the worker retries after 1s, 2s and 4s. Nobody in the checkout request waits for this.
Without this line the handler runs inside the web request, and the warehouse's outage becomes ours.

blocks.title: What it costs
items: The order is saved first, the message sent after. If the app crashes in between, the order exists and nobody is told. The outbox pattern closes that gap.
A message can arrive twice, so the handler must be idempotent.
The warehouse catches up a little later. If the user must see the result on the same screen, don't use messaging.

items.desc: start the worker that handles the queue
list messages parked on the failure shelf
send the parked messages through again

items.label: Never lose the message: the outbox

check.q: With no routing line for `OrderPlaced`, where does its handler run, and what happens if the warehouse is down?
check.a: It runs inside our own request, so the failure reaches the user, just like RPC. With a route to `async`, the message waits in the queue and a worker handles it later.

slides.title: Which one, when: three questions
slides.tldr: Do you need the answer now, are both sides up at once, and how big is the data? Those three questions are enough to choose a style.

blocks.caption: Questions for choosing a style

steps.title: 1. Need the answer now?
steps.body: If yes, RPC; if not, messaging or files
steps.tip: If a user is sitting at the screen waiting for the answer, use RPC. Otherwise it can happen later.

steps.title: 2. Other side always up?
steps.body: If not, messaging; trust RPC less
steps.tip: Our work shouldn't stop when the other side is down or slow.

steps.title: 3. Big, regular data?
steps.body: If yes, a file (batch); otherwise a message
steps.tip: 100,000 calls at 50ms each, one after another, take about 83 minutes. One file with the same rows takes seconds.

steps.title: 4. Touching their table?
steps.body: Never; use an API or an event
steps.tip: A shared DB is only for a read-only replica, never for writes, and even then in a limited scope.

blocks.caption: What fits where

columns.title: RPC / HTTP API
items: Checking a balance, validating a card
A user is waiting for the answer
Always needs a timeout and retries
columns.tip: An answer now, a small request, a direct result.

columns.title: Messaging
items: Email, stock counts, reports
Several consumers take the same news
Handlers must be idempotent
columns.tip: Spread out the work, a loose tie, a delay is fine.

columns.title: File transfer
items: Salaries, statements, nightly batches
The only way in with a legacy system
Needs a checksum and a control total
columns.tip: Big batches, a relaxed schedule, banks or government systems.

blocks.body: Never write into another system's database. Pick a contract: an API, a message or a file.

use: Shared DB: between parts of one app owned by one team, and during a temporary migration
avoid: Between separate teams or separate apps, especially for writes

check.q: A bank sends a statement of 100,000 rows each night. RPC or a file, and why?
check.a: A file. The data is big, regular, and nobody needs an answer right now. Making 100,000 separate calls would be slow and expensive.
